hub.lede: The nine towns and townships on this page are home to 100,905 people (2021 Census), and 34% of their houses were built before 1961. This guide covers 19 communities, from Owen Sound, Meaford, Hanover and Thornbury to the smallest hamlets, with the local numbers that shape an energy audit or a home health test.

cards.text: 100,905 people and 50,183 private dwellings in 2021, up 7.5% in population since 2016. On census day (May 11, 2021), 16% of the 50,183 private dwellings in Grey County were not anyone's permanent home.

Of the 36,295 houses in Grey County (single-detached, semi-detached, row houses, duplexes and mobile homes), 34% were built before 1961 and 69% before 1991, according to the 2021 Census. The typical house dates from 1971–1980.

Environment and Climate Change Canada's 1981–2010 climate normal at Thornbury Slama (27.4 km from the middle of the area) is 4,188 heating degree-days a year, with a January mean of −6.3°C. The building code's 2.5% January design temperatures for the area run from −19°C to −22°C.

In Health Canada’s 2012 survey, 11.1% of 99 homes tested in the Grey Bruce Health Unit were above the guideline. The larger 2024 Cross-Canada survey reports 12.4% (1 in 8) of homes at or above the guideline for Ontario as a whole.

Free bacteria testing for private drinking-water systems, run by Public Health Ontario. Kits are picked up and samples dropped off at 14 Grey-Bruce locations, including Owen Sound and Walkerton; a Public Health Ontario courier collects Grey County samples on Thursdays.
NRCan's list (checked October 8, 2026) shows 21 service organizations registered for postal codes in Owen Sound, Meaford and Hanover. Confirm they travel to your community.

Province-wide, 58% of Ontario households heat mainly with natural gas, 18% with electricity, 4% with propane and 1% each with oil and wood (Statistics Canada, 2023); there's no published breakdown for this area alone.

home-energy-audit.h1: Home energy audits in Grey County
home-energy-audit.title: Home energy audits and EnerGuide evaluations in Grey County: Owen Sound, Meaford, Hanover, Thornbury
home-energy-audit.description: Book a home energy assessment (EnerGuide evaluation) in Grey County: 21 NRCan-registered organizations list Owen Sound, Meaford and Hanover postal codes, 69% of local houses predate 1991, plus Ontario rebates.
home-energy-audit.lede: 21 NRCan-registered service organizations list postal codes in Owen Sound, Meaford and Hanover, and 69% of the 36,295 houses in Grey County were built before 1991. Here's what an EnerGuide evaluation costs, what it tends to find in local houses, and which Ontario rebates it unlocks, from Owen Sound, Meaford, Hanover and Thornbury to the smallest hamlet.

glance.sub: for Owen Sound, Meaford and 1 more

sections.h2: What an evaluation finds in Grey County
sections.html:
Of the 36,295 houses in Grey County (single-detached, semi-detached, row houses, duplexes and mobile homes), 34% were built before 1961 and 69% before 1991, according to the 2021 Census. The typical house here dates from 1971–1980. An EnerGuide evaluation is how you find out what that means for yours: the blower door measures air leakage, the advisor inspects the attic, walls, basement, windows and heating system, and the report ranks upgrades by what they'd save.

Environment and Climate Change Canada's 1981–2010 climate normal at Thornbury Slama (27.4 km from the middle of the area) is 4,188 heating degree-days a year, with a January mean of −6.3°C. The more heating a climate needs, the more each fix is worth, which is why the ranked list in the report matters.

On census day (May 11, 2021), 16% of the 50,183 private dwellings in Grey County were not anyone's permanent home. If you're evaluating a cottage or a house you're about to buy, tell the advisor how and when it's heated; the report models the house as a year-round home.

Province-wide, 58% of Ontario households heat mainly with natural gas, 18% with electricity, 4% with propane and 1% each with oil and wood (Statistics Canada, 2023); there's no published breakdown for this area alone. The heating system on the report shapes the recommendations: a furnace with ducts invites a ducted heat pump, electric baseboards a ductless one.

sections.h2: What it costs in Grey County
sections.html:
Typical Ontario prices are about $500–$700 for the initial EnerGuide evaluation and $200–$450 for the follow-up, plus HST where it applies. Windfall Ecology Centre charges $500 + HST for the initial evaluation and $250 + HST for the follow-up, Reep Green Solutions charges $540 and $406 with no HST, and City-backed programs in Ottawa and London quote $500–$700 as typical for the first visit. Only assessments from the seven HRSP-approved organizations qualify for the $600 Home Renovation Savings rebate, and none of the seven publishes a price.

All seven organizations approved for Home Renovation Savings assessments are among them, and only their assessments qualify for its $600 rebate. Check the HRSP-approved tag in the list below.

Most providers quote the initial (pre-upgrade) and follow-up (post-upgrade) visits separately, and organizations based in a city may add a travel fee for rural addresses. Rebate programs that pay on measured improvement need both visits, so ask for the combined price, travel included.

sections.h2: How a home energy assessment works
sections.html:
• Initial evaluation, about 2–3 hours. The advisor measures and inspects the house and runs the blower door test.
  • Report and EnerGuide rating. You get the home's energy rating and a list of recommended upgrades with estimated savings.
  • Do the work. Most rebate programs only count upgrades done after the initial evaluation.
  • Follow-up evaluation. A second visit measures the improvement, which is what most rebates pay on.

Read more: What a home energy audit involves.

heat-loss-calculation.h1: Heat loss calculations in Grey County
heat-loss-calculation.title: CSA F280-12 heat loss calculations in Grey County: Owen Sound, Meaford, Hanover, Thornbury
heat-loss-calculation.description: Room-by-room CSA F280-12 heat loss calculations for Grey County homes, sized to design temperatures of −19°C to −22°C: why it matters for heat pumps, what it costs and who does it locally.
heat-loss-calculation.lede: A heat loss calculation is how a heat pump or furnace gets sized, and its key input is the design temperature. In Grey County, the National Building Code's 2.5% January design temperatures run from −19°C at Owen Sound to −22°C at Dundalk, so a calculation for a house near Dundalk starts from a colder number than one near Owen Sound. Here's what that means for Owen Sound, Meaford and Hanover and the rest of the area.

sections.h2: Design temperatures across Grey County
sections.html:
The National Building Code of Canada 2020 says the 2.5% January design temperature is the value ordinarily used to design heating systems. Its climate table lists these Ontario locations in or next to Grey County:

Location in the code’s tableJanuary 2.5% design temperatureHeating degree-days
Owen Sound−19°C4,030
Markdale−20°C4,500
Durham−20°C4,340
Dundalk−22°C4,700
Hanover−19°C4,300

Environment and Climate Change Canada's 1981–2010 climate normal at Thornbury Slama (27.4 km from the middle of the area) is 4,188 heating degree-days a year, with a January mean of −6.3°C.

sections.h2: What CSA F280-12 asks for
sections.html:
The code requires the heating capacity for a house to be worked out with CSA F280, using the code's own design temperatures, and its list of referenced documents names the 2012 edition, CSA F280-12. The calculation works out how much heat each room loses on the design day, from the house's actual walls, windows, ceiling insulation and air leakage.

At −19°C to −22°C, a cold-climate heat pump sized to the calculation can carry most of the season, and the number shows how much backup heat the coldest days need.

sections.h2: What the calculation needs from your house
sections.html:
Of the 36,295 houses in Grey County (single-detached, semi-detached, row houses, duplexes and mobile homes), 34% were built before 1961 and 69% before 1991, according to the 2021 Census. In an older or renovated house, the walls, windows and air leakage rarely match the original plans, so ask the designer to measure rather than assume. Have this ready:

  • Room dimensions and ceiling heights, or a floor plan.
  • Window and door sizes and types, room by room.
  • Insulation levels in the attic, walls, basement and any floor over an unheated space.
  • A blower door result from an EnerGuide evaluation, if you've had one.
  • Where the ducts, radiators or baseboards run, so the heat can be delivered room by room.

sections.h2: What it costs
sections.html: There's no standard published price for a standalone F280 calculation, so ask two or three providers for a written quote that names the deliverable: the room-by-room F280 report, not just an equipment size. Many energy advisors bundle it with an EnerGuide evaluation, which also gives the calculation measured air-leakage data instead of an assumption. Ask whether a rural travel fee applies. The CSA F280 heat-loss calculation explains the method and typical cost bands.

faq.q: What design temperature is used for heat pump sizing in Owen Sound?
faq.a: The National Building Code 2020's climate table gives −19°C for Owen Sound, −20°C for Markdale, −20°C for Durham, −22°C for Dundalk and −19°C for Hanover. Provincial codes can use their own climate tables, so ask which value the calculation uses.

faq.q: What is CSA F280-12?
faq.a: The 2012 edition of CSA F280, Determining the required capacity of residential space heating and cooling appliances. The National Building Code 2020 requires heating capacity for a house to be determined with it.

faq.q: How much does a heat loss calculation cost?
faq.a: There is no standard published price. Ask two or three providers for a written quote for the F280 report, and ask whether it costs less bundled with an EnerGuide evaluation and whether a travel fee applies.

faq.q: Who does F280 calculations in Grey County?
faq.a: Many of the 21 NRCan-registered organizations that list Owen Sound, Meaford and Hanover postal codes offer them, as do HVAC designers. Ask for the F280 report itself, not just an equipment size.

radon-testing.h1: Radon testing and long-term monitoring in Grey County
radon-testing.title: Radon testing and long-term monitoring in Grey County: Owen Sound, Meaford, Hanover
radon-testing.description: Radon in Grey County: 11.1% of 99 homes tested in the Grey Bruce Health Unit were above the guideline in Health Canada's survey. How to run a 91-day long-term test, where to borrow a monitor, and mitigation by C-NRPP professionals.
radon-testing.lede: Radon is invisible, has no smell, and is the second-leading cause of lung cancer in Canada. In Health Canada's national survey, 11.1% of 99 homes tested in the Grey Bruce Health Unit were above the guideline; the larger 2024 Cross-Canada survey reports 12.4% (1 in 8) of homes at or above the guideline for Ontario as a whole. Only a long-term test tells you about your own house, in Owen Sound, Meaford and Hanover or anywhere else in Grey County.

sections.h2: Radon in Grey County
sections.html:
In Health Canada’s 2012 survey, 11.1% of 99 homes tested in the Grey Bruce Health Unit were above the guideline. The survey used the health regions of the time; today the area is served by Grey Bruce Public Health.

The larger 2024 Cross-Canada survey reports 12.4% (1 in 8) of homes at or above the guideline for Ontario as a whole. The two surveys aren't directly comparable: the 2024 study pooled about 69,000 volunteer tests, more of them in basements, which partly explains its higher numbers. Neither can tell you about a single house, because neighbouring homes can differ widely.

Grey Bruce Public Health says parts of Grey and Bruce counties have the potential to be high-risk for radon, based on a radon potential map (created in 2012, updated in 2017). It recommends a three-month long-term kit, which it says costs about $40–$60 online or at building stores, retesting every few years, and retesting after any fix; it puts repair costs at anywhere from a few hundred dollars to several thousand.

sections.h2: Long-term monitoring: how to test properly
sections.html:
Health Canada's measurement guide asks for a long-term test with at least 91 days in the heating season, when closed windows and the stack effect make readings higher, so the result is a conservative estimate of the yearly average. It recommends testing for 3 to 12 months.

  • Alpha track detectors record radon's alpha particles on a plastic film; you mail them to a lab when the test ends.
  • Electret ion chambers lose charge as radon ionizes the air inside; a lab reads the voltage drop.
  • Digital (electronic) monitors read continuously and show results on a screen or an app. For a long-term test, Health Canada says to use one that has passed C-NRPP performance testing, and it still has to run at least three months.

Place the detector on the lowest level where someone spends more than four hours a day, at least 30 cm above the floor and 30 cm from walls, and at least 1 m from vents, windows and doors; avoid kitchens, laundry rooms and bathrooms. A digital monitor left running after mitigation lets you watch for changes between the long-term tests below.

sections.h2: Kits, lending libraries and professionals
sections.html:
• There's no provincial free-kit program, but many Ontario public libraries lend digital radon monitors free with a library card, among them Hamilton, Vaughan, Guelph, Kingston Frontenac, Greater Sudbury, Thunder Bay, Brantford and Waterloo.
  • For a professional measurement or mitigation, search the C-NRPP directory ↗ by postal code; it lists certified measurement and mitigation professionals, and you can confirm they cover Owen Sound and the rest of Grey County.

sections.h2: If your level is high: mitigation
sections.html:
Health Canada recommends fixing levels above 200 Bq/m³ within a year, and sooner the higher the level. The usual fix is a sub-slab depressurization system (a sealed pipe through the floor and a fan venting outside), which Health Canada says costs about $2,000 to $3,000 including material and labour and cuts radon by more than 80% in most homes. Hire a professional certified for mitigation under C-NRPP.

After a system goes in:

  • A C-NRPP professional runs a short test starting at least 24 hours after the fan is turned on.
  • A long-term three-month test follows in the next fall or winter, done by a company other than the installer.
  • With an active system, Health Canada recommends a long-term test within two years of activation and every five years after that, and again after renovations.
  • Check the system's pressure gauge (manometer) regularly and never switch the fan off. It costs about $50 to $75 a year to run; a replacement fan is $200 to $300.

Since January 1, 2025, the Ontario Building Code requires new houses to include a soil-gas barrier and a radon rough-in. Tarion's new-home warranty covers radon remediation for seven years from possession, and the Canadian Lung Association's Lungs Matter program offers up to $1,500 toward mitigation for households with low to moderate incomes or a lung cancer diagnosis.

Read more: The radon testing guide.

faq.q: Is radon a problem in Grey County?
faq.a: In Health Canada’s 2012 survey, 11.1% of 99 homes tested in the Grey Bruce Health Unit were above the guideline. The larger 2024 Cross-Canada survey reports 12.4% (1 in 8) of homes at or above the guideline for Ontario as a whole. Any home can have high radon, so Health Canada recommends testing every home.

faq.q: How long should a radon test take?
faq.a: At least three months, with at least 91 days in the heating season. Health Canada recommends 3 to 12 months; short tests can’t give your long-term average.

faq.q: Where can I get a radon monitor or kit in Owen Sound?
faq.a: There's no provincial free-kit program, but many Ontario public libraries lend digital radon monitors free with a library card, among them Hamilton, Vaughan, Guelph, Kingston Frontenac, Greater Sudbury, Thunder Bay, Brantford and Waterloo. Long-term kits are also sold online and at hardware stores.

faq.q: What does radon mitigation cost?
faq.a: Health Canada puts a sub-slab depressurization system at about $2,000 to $3,000 including material and labour, plus about $50 to $75 a year to run the fan.

faq.q: Should I keep monitoring after mitigation?
faq.a: Yes. Health Canada recommends a long-term test the following heating season, another within two years of activation, and one every five years after that. A digital monitor running in between shows if anything changes.

mold-testing.h1: Mould and indoor air quality testing in Grey County
mold-testing.title: Mould and indoor air quality (IAQ) testing in Grey County: Owen Sound, Meaford, Hanover
mold-testing.description: Mould inspection and indoor air quality testing in Grey County, where 69% of houses were built before 1991: when mold sampling helps, the cleanup size rules from CMHC and Health Canada, and when to hire a remediation contractor.
mold-testing.lede: 69% of the 36,295 houses in Grey County were built before 1991, and winters here bring about 4,188 heating degree-days a year: cold corners and older basements are where mould usually starts. Here's how to inspect for it in Owen Sound, Meaford, Hanover and Thornbury, when air sampling helps, and when cleanup is a job for a contractor.

glance.sub: or if it keeps coming back

sections.h2: Why mould shows up in Grey County homes
sections.html:
Environment and Climate Change Canada's 1981–2010 climate normal at Thornbury Slama (27.4 km from the middle of the area) is 4,188 heating degree-days a year, with a January mean of −6.3°C. On cold days, exterior corners, closets on outside walls and window frames get cold enough for condensation, which is where mould often starts.

Of the 36,295 houses in Grey County (single-detached, semi-detached, row houses, duplexes and mobile homes), 34% were built before 1961 and 69% before 1991, according to the 2021 Census. Older basements without a moisture barrier, and houses air-sealed without adding ventilation, are common trouble spots.

On census day (May 11, 2021), 16% of the 50,183 private dwellings in Grey County were not anyone's permanent home. A house or cottage that sits closed up for long stretches is worth a sniff test and a look in the basement each time you open it.

sections.h2: Mould inspection: when sampling helps
sections.html:
Start by looking and smelling: stains, discoloured patches, peeling paint and a musty odour, especially in basements, bathrooms, window frames and closets on outside walls. Health Canada says measuring mould concentrations or identifying species is usually unnecessary: if you can see or smell it, fix the moisture and clean up.

Air or surface sampling helps when you smell mustiness but can't find the source, after a leak or flood to check the cleanup worked, or before buying a house with signs of past water damage. Ask which lab analyzes the samples and look for one accredited under AIHA's EMLAP program.

sections.h2: Cleanup and remediation: the size rules
sections.html:
CMHC and Health Canada sort mould by size, and the size decides who should clean it up:

SizeWhat countsWho should clean it
SmallOne to three patches, each smaller than 1 m²A healthy homeowner, with water and unscented dish detergent (CMHC)
MediumMore than three patches, or patches between 1 and 3 m² (32 square feet)Trained help; homeowners only with training and precautions
LargeA patch larger than 3 m², or many patches through the houseA qualified mould remediation contractor (CMHC)
  • Fix the moisture source first: a leak, poor drainage, or condensation from high humidity. Health Canada recommends 30–50% relative humidity.
  • For a small cleanup, wear safety glasses or goggles, an N95 mask if possible and household rubber gloves. People at risk from mould shouldn't clean it and should stay away.
  • Health Canada suggests professional help for extensive mould, especially growth that keeps coming back after cleaning.

sections.h2: Choosing a tester or contractor
sections.html:
Ask any tester which lab analyzes their samples and what the report will recommend; a good report points to the moisture source. For remediation, get two or three written quotes that describe containment, what will be removed and how the area is cleaned. No province has a mandatory mould standard for homes, and Health Canada sets no numerical limit.

Read more: The mould and indoor air quality guide.

faq.q: Do I need mould testing in Grey County if I can see mould?
faq.a: Usually not. Visible mould needs cleanup and a fix for the moisture source. Sampling helps most when you suspect mould you can’t see.

faq.q: How much mould can I clean myself?
faq.a: CMHC says a healthy homeowner can clean one to three patches, each under 1 m², with water and unscented dish detergent. Larger areas need trained help or a remediation contractor.

faq.q: When should I hire a mould remediation contractor?
faq.a: For a single patch over 3 m², many patches through the house, or mould that keeps coming back after cleaning (CMHC, Health Canada).

faq.q: Is there a legal mould limit for homes in Canada?
faq.a: No. Health Canada sets no numerical limit; its guidance is to control moisture and clean up mould.

well-water-testing.title: Well water testing in Grey County: free bacteria (E. coli and coliform) tests in Owen Sound, Meaford, Hanover
well-water-testing.description: Private well testing in Grey County: free bacteria tests for E. coli and total coliforms through Grey Bruce Public Health, where to pick up bottles and drop off samples, how often to test, and chemistry such as nitrate.
well-water-testing.lede: Homes on private wells in Grey County, from Owen Sound, Meaford and Hanover to the smallest hamlets, can test for bacteria (E. coli and total coliforms) for free through Grey Bruce Public Health, with bottle pick-up and drop-off in Owen Sound and Walkerton. Here's how the local program works, how often to test, and what the free test doesn't cover.

sections.h2: Free testing through Grey Bruce Public Health
sections.html:
Free bacteria testing for private drinking-water systems, run by Public Health Ontario. Kits are picked up and samples dropped off at 14 Grey-Bruce locations, including Owen Sound and Walkerton; a Public Health Ontario courier collects Grey County samples on Thursdays.

Grey Bruce Public Health recommends testing at least three times a year, after any work on your well or water system and after significant weather events.

sections.h2: What the free test covers, and what it doesn’t
sections.html: Public Health Ontario's lab tests only for indicator bacteria: total coliforms and E. coli. Samples have to reach the lab within a day or two, so collect them early in the week and check the drop-off cut-off times. Chemicals, metals and minerals need a private lab; nitrate testing is recommended, especially if an infant will drink the water.

sections.h2: Reading the results, and what to do next
sections.html:
Ontario's guide to testing and treating private wells reads the counts (per 100 mL) like this:

  • E. coli above 0: unsafe to drink, with evidence of animal or human waste getting into the well. Stop drinking the water and call the health unit right away.
  • Total coliforms above 5, no E. coli: significant evidence of bacterial contamination, usually surface water getting in. The water may be unsafe to drink: call the health unit, inspect and repair the well, shock-chlorinate it if needed and retest.
  • Total coliforms of 5 or fewer, no E. coli: some evidence of bacteria, which may not be significant at these low levels. Keep testing to track the pattern.

Boiling water at a rolling boil for at least one minute kills harmful organisms but doesn't remove dissolved contaminants. To disinfect, the province says to shock-chlorinate the well and the entire household plumbing system. Between tests, check that the well cap and the sealant around the casing aren't cracked or damaged, and keep the ground sloping away from the well: Ontario's Wells Regulation requires owners to maintain a well so surface water can't get in.

sections.h2: Why testing is worth the trip
sections.html: Ontario's auditor general estimated in 2025 that about 1.3 million Ontarians rely on private wells, and that fewer than a third of well owners had tested in the previous 12 months (as reported by CBC). Well water can change with the seasons, after heavy rain or snowmelt, and after work on the well, which is why the health units ask for several tests a year.

sections.h2: What to test for
sections.html:
• Bacteria (total coliforms and E. coli), several times a year and after flooding, heavy rain or work on the well.
  • Nitrate, especially near farmland or septic systems: the province flags nitrate above 10 ppm as a health risk for infants, and reverse osmosis or distillation treats it.
  • Naturally occurring minerals such as arsenic, uranium and radium, which the province lists as long-term health risks; a private accredited lab tests for them.

Read more: The well water guide.

faq.q: Is well water testing free in Grey County?
faq.a: Yes for bacteria. Free bacteria testing for private drinking-water systems, run by Public Health Ontario. Chemicals, metals and minerals need a private lab; nitrate testing is recommended, especially if an infant will drink the water.

faq.q: Where do I get a well water bottle in Owen Sound?
faq.a: Kits are picked up and samples dropped off at 14 Grey-Bruce locations, including Owen Sound and Walkerton; a Public Health Ontario courier collects Grey County samples on Thursdays.

faq.q: How often should I test my well?
faq.a: Grey Bruce Public Health recommends testing at least three times a year, after any work on your well or water system and after significant weather events.

faq.q: Does the free test check for nitrate?
faq.a: Chemicals, metals and minerals need a private lab; nitrate testing is recommended, especially if an infant will drink the water.

faq.q: What if my well water test shows E. coli?
faq.a: Ontario says any E. coli means the water is unsafe to drink. Stop drinking it, use bottled water, and call your public health unit right away; it will advise on repairs, shock chlorination and retesting.

wood-burning-inspection.h1: Wood-burning appliance inspections (WETT) in Grey County
wood-burning-inspection.title: WETT-certified wood stove and chimney inspections in Grey County: Owen Sound, Meaford, Hanover
wood-burning-inspection.description: Wood-burning appliance (WETT) inspections in Grey County: what an inspection checks, how to find a WETT-certified inspector, certified stoves, and the Ontario Fire Code rule for a chimney inspection every 12 months.
wood-burning-inspection.lede: Ontario's Fire Code requires every chimney, flue and flue pipe to be inspected at least once every 12 months, when an appliance is added and after any chimney fire. In Grey County, with about 4,188 heating degree-days a year, a wood stove or insert can run for much of the year. Here's what an inspection covers and how to book a WETT-certified inspector in Owen Sound, Meaford, Hanover and Thornbury or anywhere else in the area.

sections.h2: Why inspections matter in Grey County
sections.html:
Environment and Climate Change Canada's 1981–2010 climate normal at Thornbury Slama (27.4 km from the middle of the area) is 4,188 heating degree-days a year, with a January mean of −6.3°C. Of the 36,295 houses in Grey County (single-detached, semi-detached, row houses, duplexes and mobile homes), 34% were built before 1961 and 69% before 1991, according to the 2021 Census.

On census day (May 11, 2021), 16% of the 50,183 private dwellings in Grey County were not anyone's permanent home. If you're buying a cottage or a house with a wood stove, ask your insurer what inspection it needs before the deal closes.

WETT Inc., the non-profit that trains and registers wood-energy professionals across Canada, says hiring a WETT-certified professional ensures wood-burning appliances are inspected, installed and maintained to current safety codes and standards, and helps homeowners meet insurance or regulatory requirements.

sections.h2: What a wood-burning inspection checks
sections.html:
An inspection looks at what the fire and installation codes regulate:

  • The chimney, flue and flue pipe: structural problems such as a missing liner or inadequate supports, and decay such as cracking, crumbling mortar, corrosion or separated sections (National Fire Code notes).
  • Creosote and soot: deposits more than 3 mm thick mean the chimney needs cleaning right away and should be inspected more often.
  • Clearances: the required space between the appliance, flue pipe or chimney and anything combustible, which must be kept clear.
  • The installation: CSA B365 is the installation code for solid-fuel appliances, covering installation, alteration and maintenance.
  • The appliance itself: whether it's certified to CSA B415.1 or the US EPA standard, which you can usually tell from its label or plate.

sections.h2: Finding a WETT-certified inspector
sections.html: Search the WETT directory ↗ for certified professionals near Owen Sound and the rest of Grey County, and ask your home insurer what it needs to see when you add a stove or buy a house that has one. WETT doesn't publish inspection prices, so get two or three written quotes and ask what each inspection includes.

sections.h2: Keeping it safe between inspections
sections.html:
• Burn dry wood: the US EPA says wood burns best below 20% moisture; check it with a moisture meter.
  • Dense smoke at the top of the chimney is a warning sign of poor operation, a wrongly sized chimney or unsuitable fuel (National Fire Code note).
  • Keep combustible things out of the clearance space around the stove and flue pipe.
  • Have the chimney inspected after any chimney fire, and when you add or replace an appliance.

Read the full wood-burning inspection guide.

faq.q: How often should a wood stove chimney be inspected in Grey County?
faq.a: Ontario's Fire Code requires every chimney, flue and flue pipe to be inspected at least once every 12 months, when an appliance is added and after any chimney fire, and cleaned as often as needed to keep combustible deposits from building up.

faq.q: What is a WETT inspection?
faq.a: An inspection of a wood-burning appliance and its chimney or venting by a professional certified through the WETT program, which WETT Inc. says helps homeowners meet insurance or regulatory requirements.

faq.q: How do I find a WETT-certified inspector near Owen Sound?
faq.a: Search the WETT directory on wettinc.ca, then confirm the inspector covers your address and ask what the inspection includes.

faq.q: How much does a WETT inspection cost?
faq.a: WETT doesn’t publish prices and we found no reliable published range, so ask two or three inspectors for written quotes.

faq.q: What is a certified wood stove?
faq.a: One tested to CSA B415.1 or certified by the US EPA for emissions. The EPA’s 2020 limit for new room heaters is 2.0 grams of particles per hour (crib wood) or 2.5 g/h (cord wood).
